content: Schistosoma haematobium eggs and granuloma formation in the walls of the urinary bladder can lead to lower urinary tract symptoms, including haematuria, increased frequency of urination, and dysuria. Complications may include bladder calcification, urinary tract fibrosis causing obstructive uropathy, and bladder cancer. Infection with Schistosoma haematobium is also a significant cause of female genital schistosomiasis, which increases the risk of HIV transmission. Intestinal schistosomiasis is caused by Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum, whose eggs are typically trapped in the walls of the large intestine, rectum, and liver. Symptoms include abdominal pain, alternating diarrhea and constipation, and occult blood in the feces. Granuloma formation due to egg deposition in the liver can result in periportal fibrosis, leading to advanced disease characterized by portal hypertension and hepatosplenomegaly. Serious complications at this stage include ascites and variceal bleeding, which can be fatal. All schistosome species can affect the lungs and reproductive organs. In children, schistosomiasis may lead to growth retardation, anemia, impaired cognition, poor school performance, and reduced physical fitness. Currently, there is no definitive gold standard test for diagnosing schistosomiasis. Diagnosis primarily relies on microscopic detection of viable eggs in stool (for Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum) or urine (for Schistosoma haematobium). The Kato-Katz technique is widely used for diagnosing and quantifying the prevalence and intensity of Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum infections. This involves preparing a thick smear of filtered stool, staining it, and examining it under a microscope to count eggs, which are then multiplied by a factor to estimate the number of eggs per gram of stool. Infection intensity is categorized as light, moderate, or heavy based on World Health Organization (WHO) classifications. For Schistosoma haematobium infections, a 10 mL mid-day urine sample is filtered through a polycarbonate filter, and trapped eggs are stained and counted under a microscope. Infection intensity is expressed as the number of eggs per 10 mL of urine, with a threshold of 50 eggs distinguishing between light and heavy infections. Both the Kato-Katz and urine filtration methods have low sensitivity for detecting very low-intensity infections and present challenges related to sample handling. Other diagnostic methods, such as the FLOTAC technique, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), circulating anodic antigen (CAA), and point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen (CCA), show promise but are less commonly used. Ultrasound can assess schistosomiasis-induced organ morbidity. In the absence of a safe and effective vaccine, the WHO recommends a schistosomiasis control strategy called preventive chemotherapy. This involves administering regular (usually annual) single doses of praziquantel to at-risk populations, regardless of infection status. Praziquantel is the drug of choice for schistosomiasis prevention because it is effective against all schistosome species, can be administered as a single oral dose, is affordable, and has a relatively safe profile. Common side effects of praziquantel are mild and transient, including nausea, dizziness, pruritus, skin rash, headache, drowsiness, and abdominal pain. However, the large size and bitter taste of praziquantel tablets make them unsuitable for young children. The goal of preventive chemotherapy is to control schistosomiasis-related morbidity by 2020 and eliminate schistosomiasis as a public health problem by 2025. Preventive chemotherapy is often delivered through schoolor community-wide distribution channels as part of large-scale targeted treatment programs. In high-risk communities (baseline prevalence ≥50%), all school-aged children and at-risk adults receive annual praziquantel treatment. In moderate-risk communities (baseline prevalence 10–49%), school-aged children and special-risk groups are treated biennially. In low-risk communities (baseline prevalence <10%), school-aged children receive praziquantel treatment twice during their primary schooling. The success of large-scale targeted treatment depends on treatment frequency, coverage levels, compliance, and sociocultural factors. To reduce schistosomiasis-related morbidity in high-risk areas and eliminate it in low-risk areas, the World Health Assembly has urged member states to increase annual treatment coverage for school-aged children to at least 75–100%. Preventive chemotherapy aims to achieve three major goals: controlling morbidity by reducing the prevalence of heavy-intensity infections to less than 5%, eliminating schistosomiasis as a public health problem by reducing heavy-intensity infections to less than 1%, and interrupting transmission by reducing the incidence of schistosomiasis to zero. To ensure sustainability and avoid dependence on mass drug administration, intervention strategies should integrate preventive chemotherapy with vector control, provision of clean water, adequate sanitation, and community health education to promote behavior change. Preventive chemotherapy for schistosomiasis relies on praziquantel, whose mechanism of action is poorly understood. While praziquantel is effective against adult schistosome worms, it is not 100% curative, does not prevent reinfection, and is ineffective against juvenile stages of the parasite (schistosomula). An annual standard dose of 40 mg/kg of praziquantel is recommended for preventive treatment in adults and school-aged children with confirmed infections or at risk of infection. Cure rates after a single dose of praziquantel range from 60% to 90% and are inversely related to infection intensity. Mass administration of praziquantel to at-risk groups in endemic areas reduces schistosome egg excretion, environmental contamination, and snail population infection, thereby minimizing the source of human infection. Treatment with praziquantel can reduce worm burden, infection intensity, and schistosomiasis-associated morbidity in treated individuals.
